# 16. Production and process

This chapter is about how roguelikes actually get made: choosing a first project, finding the seed a game grows from, prototyping, generating and cutting ideas, estimating, paying for procedural content, playtesting, working with a live audience, organising small teams and their tools, keeping yourself going, and looking after a game that outlives its first developer. Most roguelikes are made by one person or a handful, often part-time and often over many years, so these are not side issues. Whether a design ever reaches players depends on them.

The talks approach production as practitioners rather than theorists. They are postmortems, confessions of projects that died, and working methods shared by people who shipped. Read together, they converge on a short list of habits: finish something small, test the core before building around it, cut what does not serve it, assume the schedule is wrong, and put other people's play at the centre of development rather than at the end. Where they disagree, on how much to plan, how long code should live, how to watch a playtest or when to stop building a game, the disagreement usually turns on the size and purpose of the project, and the chapter tries to say which.

## In brief

- Finish a small, complete game before the dream project: only a finished game earns feedback and teaches the whole development process, and a project allowed to die still passes its lessons to the next ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 4:14](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=254); [Josh Ge 2018, 4:16](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=256); [Jeff Lait 2025, 3:20](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=200); [slashie 2026, 9:05:28](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32728)).
- Build outward from a seed you can test within weeks, whether a core mechanic you can state in one sentence or a feeling you want the player to have, and prototype that before anything around it ([Josh Ge 2018, 5:50](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=350); [Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 15:17](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=917); [Nic Tringali 2023, 26:21](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1581)).
- Prototype in the cheapest medium that answers the question (a spreadsheet, paper, a day of code), and decide explicitly when the prototype ends, because otherwise its code becomes the product ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 2:00](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=120); [Brian Cronin 2025, 1:48](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=108); [David Brevik 2023, 10:06](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=606); [Brian Cronin 2021, 5:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=305); [Brian Cronin 2024, 4:57](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=297)).
- Hold every system to the core of the game, including genre staples you assume you need, and in a roguelike ask whether it makes runs differ from each other ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 4:48](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=288); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 11:06](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=666); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 12:11](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=731); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 7:51](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=471)).
- Assume every estimate is far too low, since the cases run over at every scale; one designer's rule is to multiply by four, then by four again ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 10:37](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=637); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 30:52](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1852); [Thomas Biskup 2016, 5:15](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=315); [Josh Ge 2016, 14:20](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=860); [Jeff Olson 2023, 20:52](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=1252)).
- Procedural generation is not a shortcut to cheap content: budget for honing output to quality, writing in components, validating what the generator can produce and localising generated text ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 30:06](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1806); [Leigh Alexander 2023, 27:41](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1661); [Jurie Horneman 2023, 22:48](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1368); [Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:56:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6982)).
- You cannot judge your own game's fun or clarity, so make playtesting the centre of development: small rounds of three to five testers, watched live, with at least one change after each ([Brian Cronin 2025, 7:40](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=460); [Brian Cronin 2025, 13:16](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=796); [Brian Cronin 2025, 15:26](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=926); [Santiago Zapata 2016, 12:46](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=766); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 19:09](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1149)).
- Player feedback pays only when someone triages it consistently and the team, not the crowd, decides, treating requests as descriptions of problems rather than specifications of fixes ([Brian Cronin 2021, 18:11](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1091); [Chris King 2022, 10:09](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=609); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 17:23](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1043)).
- Make adding one more piece of content trivial and make sure nobody waits on a tool or a decision, because iteration speed is what tools and team structure are for ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 3:51](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=231); [Thomas Robertson 2021, 8:11](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=491); [Danny Day 2018, 23:36](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1416); [Thomas Biskup 2018, 4:49](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=289)).
- Sustain a long project with steady, visible progress (something new every working day, a regular slice of time rather than bursts), and keep talking to players even when you slow down ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:26](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=326); [Phillip Daigle 2020, 12:35](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=755); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 15:04](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=904); [Thomas Biskup 2016, 15:14](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=914)).

## Start small and finish: why a shipped game comes first

The most repeated piece of production advice in these talks is to finish something. Not a demo, not an engine, not a world model: a playable game, however small, that someone else can pick up. The reasoning is consistent across speakers. A finished game is the only thing that earns you feedback, and finishing is the only way to learn the whole development process, which changes character from beginning to end ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 4:14](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=254); [Josh Ge 2018, 4:16](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=256)).

Santiago Zapata tells the story from the inside. He entered his first Seven Day Roguelike challenge (7DRL, the annual jam where entrants build a roguelike in a week) thinking it a waste of time after two unproductive years, and came out with Castlevania Roguelike: not very fun, not complete, but a finished game. Without shipping, he says, you keep working on demos and technical work and never get feedback. That first game had no procedural generation at all; he learned he could build a game around a single fun feature ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 4:14](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=254)). Josh Ge gives the same advice as a rule for beginners: build a small, complete roguelike before your dream project, because you only learn by going through the entire process once or twice, and because aiming big right away makes failure more likely. A small finished game also becomes a stable foundation to expand later ([Josh Ge 2018, 4:16](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=256)). Jasper Cole's top advice from Backpack Hero is the commercial version of the same point: release something. The free itch.io version made in January 2022, followed by a Kickstarter in May, is what turned the game into the team's main focus ([Jasper Cole 2023, 27:08](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1628)).

Finishing is also a permission you have to give yourself. Jeff Lait contrasts his 7DRLs, which were actually finished, with Powder, which is not; tying the bow and walking away is hard because a creator always sees more to add, but declaring a small game complete lets you move on and try more of the design space ([Jeff Lait 2025, 3:20](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=200)).

### The failure the advice grew out of

The advice is a reaction to a specific history. When he started, Zapata says, he and many others on the Usenet roguelike development group were building world simulators inspired by ADOM and JADE. His own was a complete medieval fantasy world simulator that took about two years and produced no game; the group was building sandboxes in which "the game will rise" rather than designing a game ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 2:49](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=169)). In his historical overview he describes the broader movement, inspired by GenRogue, to make roguelikes the ultimate detailed simulation of a fantasy world, with combat modelling a hundred body parts down to the fingernails; it largely failed because the projects were too complex for their developers to finish ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 26:59](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=1619)).

Tarn and Zach Adams lived the same trap. Their early project Armok tracked every tissue, procedurally generated animations from stance points and showed muscles under stripped skin, down to the curliness of arm hair. Tarn grants there is something to starting from basic structures, but their idea was so large that all they built was data structures, and Armok never became a game; he counts hundreds of dead projects ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 11:54](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=714)).

Ge offers a picture of what this feels like from inside. Development is a dungeon. Wander toward every system you think you need and you may reach the goal at great cost, or develop yourself into a corner, get demoralised and quit. Instead, make a beeline to a fun playable game with a basic plan, then expand outward ([Josh Ge 2018, 1:23](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=83)).

### The 7DRL as the community's answer

The 7DRL is the community's institutional response. Lait recounts that it began when Joseph Hewitt, author of GearHead, made a roguelike in a week, and that it broke a design stasis: roguelikes were assumed to be ADOM- or NetHack-sized, and in a game that size design is baked in, so changing something like hit point recovery means changing the whole game. Realising a roguelike could be built in seven days gave new mechanics somewhere to be tried ([Jeff Lait 2025, 2:09](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=129)). Zapata places it in a wider shift of the 2000s, when coffee-break roguelikes and the 7DRL moved the community's mindset toward smaller, focused games; the challenge went from fewer than twenty roguelikes in the whole of the 1980s to hundreds every year, pulling in ideas from other genres, although projects aiming at great worlds such as Ultima Ratio Regum continue ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 28:56](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=1736)). David Craddock, who checked in daily with participants for his book One Week Dungeons, found a wide spectrum of designs, from an overworld crawl where the arrangement of three character archetypes decided who dealt and took damage to Darren Grey's music-oriented Mosaic ([David Craddock 2016, 18:14](https://youtu.be/Gs9Nb5ZYRY0?t=1094)).

The jam is not automatically the right first step. Ge calls the 7DRL a good way to prototype and prove a core mechanic, with over a hundred entries a year and a guaranteed audience for anyone who finishes, but he does not recommend it as a first game: you don't need that pressure so early, and the deadline helps most once you know the technical side ([Josh Ge 2018, 7:18](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=438)). Scope still bites inside a week. Zapata's Expedition, a Seven Cities of Gold-style colonisation roguelike, was impossible in seven days and shipped without its procedural generation, with only a fixed map; his lesson was to watch scope, especially when starting out ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 12:11](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=731)).

Two practitioners give concrete ways to make a week work. Zapata keeps the last day for playtesting and tweaks, gives at least two days to data such as monsters, items and quests, and spends the rest on code; first entries usually aren't good, he says, but the compressed cycle builds the skill of finishing quickly ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 24:16](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=1456)). Ge went further for Cogmind: he judged the design far too ambitious for a week and planned on paper for over a month beforehand, without which the 7DRL version would have been impossible. He adds that entrants need not work as intensely as he did ([Josh Ge 2016, 8:29](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=509)).

### Good first projects

The talks suggest several first projects that keep design questions small so you can concentrate on finishing:

- **A roguelike of a game you already know.** Ge's first roguelike was an X-COM roguelike, written after Andrew Doull's 2008 call for one. Knowing the mechanics let him focus on technical and usability problems such as showing a 3D multi-level world in a roguelike interface; many first roguelikes, he notes, turn a favourite thing into a roguelike ([Josh Ge 2016, 5:45](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=345)).
- **An "xRL" of an existing IP.** Most design questions are already answered, so you adapt the IP to roguelike formulas and get instant fans. Ge's examples are DoomRL, AliensRL, DiabloRL and his own XCOMRL, with the warning that litigious IP holders are a real risk: DoomRL was renamed DRL after a cease and desist, and he advises against an explicitly Pokémon roguelike ([Josh Ge 2018, 23:18](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1398)).
- **A Chase clone.** Dan Norder recommends the old BASIC game Chase as an entry-level project: addictive, simple, easy to make non-violent, re-themeable (PopCap's pirate-themed Seven Seas is one variant), and everything you learn carries over to a full roguelike ([Dan Norder 2024, 25:32](https://youtu.be/ohH6LBM2EiU?t=1532)).
- **robotfindskitten.** Leonard Richardson explains that it spread to so many platforms because it is a simple program that does something non-trivial and fun, which makes it a good first program on any new language or platform; Mel Chua learned to program by modifying its source to add in-jokes ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 10:43](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=643)).
- **The next small game, built on the last one.** Zapata's sequence of 7DRLs reused code each time: DrashRL took Castlevania Roguelike's code and added procedural generation, Metroid Roguelike invested in world generation, and Zelda Roguelike added an overworld generator and a more complex dungeon generator ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 4:51](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=291)).

### The counter-position: a personal project needs no rules

Not everyone accepts the rule. Phillip Daigle deliberately ignored "start small" on Rogue's Gate. His argument is that a game made purely for yourself removes commercial pressure, and when there is no pressure development stops being a chore and becomes creative expression and a way to learn your own preferences; for the same reason he would not impose arbitrary deadlines on such a project ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 23:34](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1414)). The disagreement is narrower than it looks. Ge and Zapata are advising people who want a finished, played game; Daigle is describing a project whose purpose is the making. Decide which you are doing before you decide how big to go.

### A career of small games

slashie, mapping two decades of his own projects as a network of influences, found that he had not been making separate games but running one long design experiment, each game a fragment of an answer to a few recurring design questions ([slashie 2026, 9:04:00](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32640)). He frames development itself as a roguelike: hard design questions cannot be solved in one pass, so each project should be allowed to die rather than be prolonged until it finds the answer, with its postmortem and its players' feedback carried into the next attempt as a mutation of what worked. 7DRLs and game jams helped him finish; most projects on his map took under a year, some only days ([slashie 2026, 9:05:28](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32728)).

> You got to give yourself a chance of the project dying instead of prolonging it indefinitely until you hit a solution. — [slashie 2026, 9:05:28](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32728)

Keeping a record is what makes the lineage usable. slashie's map is built from a JSON file of every project (years, collaborators, genre, links) and from his blog, records he kept mainly to pick up old work ([slashie 2026, 9:04:00](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32640)). Pippin Barr and Jonathan Lessard go further, documenting every step of making Chogue and publishing its emails, design journal and code history on GitHub, because the knowledge about design lies in the path of decisions, not only in the end result ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 6:12](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=372)).

**In practice.** Choose a first project whose design questions are mostly answered: a game you know, a Chase clone, a single fun feature. Bound it so you can finish it in weeks, not years, and leave procedural generation out if the core works without it. If you enter a 7DRL, do it after a first project, reserve the last day for playtesting, and do your heavy design on paper before the week starts. Declare it finished, write down what you learned, and carry the code and the lessons into the next one ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 24:16](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=1456); [Santiago Zapata 2016, 4:51](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=291); [slashie 2026, 9:05:28](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32728)).

## Finding the core: design goals, the one-sentence mechanic and how much to plan

If you are going to make a beeline for a playable game, you need to know what you are aiming at. The talks agree that a roguelike should grow outward from something small and testable. They differ on what that seed should be.

### Two seeds: a mechanic or a feeling

Josh Ge's seed is a core mechanic. Ask what the game's unique take is, and whether it would be fun if it had only that. The mechanic should be explainable in a single sentence, and it is what you prototype first, with only as many surrounding systems as you need to bring it out. If the repeated minute-to-minute play isn't fun, nothing built on top of it will matter ([Josh Ge 2018, 5:50](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=350)).

Subset Games starts one level higher, from an emotional state. Justin Ma and Matthew Davis describe choosing a feeling and then building whatever game best serves it, assembling their way into a genre rather than picking one first. FTL's feeling was captaining a starship like Adama or Picard; Into the Breach answered superhero films in which cities are destroyed and nobody cares, so collateral damage had to matter and you should be willing to sacrifice yourself to save the city ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 15:17](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=917)).

The two are less opposed than they sound: a feeling still has to be turned into something that can be prototyped. Phillip Daigle shows one route from the feeling end. He sketches a desired scenario as a pixel-art mock-up from his own assets, asks what mood and pressure he wants the player to feel, and once something looks worth playing asks how a player would arrive there and what systems they need, much like an agile user story ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 22:58](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1378)). Nic Tringali's The Banished Vault shows the mechanic end. Within weeks the team had a prototype of the delta-v map and movement maths, and asked one question of it: is getting from one place to another on as little fuel as possible an interesting puzzle? Survival goals came after, and the gothic monastery theme later still ([Nic Tringali 2023, 26:21](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1581)).

Tringali also warns about a quieter way to skip this step. Designers tend to assemble games from components whose feel they assume (dice feel like this, cards like that), which glosses over fine detail; he admits he is prone to designing by intuition and iterating on that intuition, which can feel like building on shaky foundations, and he does not believe a game can be designed without iteration and testing ([Nic Tringali 2026, 4:57:34](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17854)). Test the seed itself, not your belief about how it will feel.

### How much to plan

On planning, the talks split along a clear line. One side keeps the written design tiny and lets the game reveal itself. Casey Yano says Slay the Spire's design document was about two pages (deckbuilding, classes, monsters); pacing, the map, potions, relics and map node types were all discovered during development ([Casey Yano 2022, 11:04](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=664)). Daigle goes further on a personal project: start with only a vague design and build features you will later discard, because each discarded feature teaches you why something does or doesn't work. Rogue's Gate ended up dramatically different from its original plan. He is explicit that in commercial development this waste of time and resources would be a horrible idea ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 21:22](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1282)).

The other side names decisions that are expensive to change later. Dylan White argues that a game's spellcasting resource mechanics (mana bars, cooldowns, cards, regeneration and draw rates) should be settled carefully up front, because spells, items and skills get designed around them and changing them retroactively throws away a lot of work ([Dylan White 2021, 2:31](https://youtu.be/kvgKKRLil_8?t=151)). Santiago Zapata set explicit design guidelines at the start of DrashRL, no experience grinding and no commands or menus, so that he had a plan instead of improvising. The same project shows the guidelines are not a design: his original ant-colony simulator idea produced no fun mechanic in research, and he switched to a survival arena that worked much better ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 5:24](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=324)).

Ge's description of how roguelikes are built sits between the two. A roguelike is a conglomeration of systems that can be tacked on one at a time when they support the game, then expanded and iterated with player feedback; all you need is a plan and perseverance ([Josh Ge 2018, 5:08](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=308)). That structure is what lets a small design document work: the core is decided, everything else can be added later. White's warning marks the exception, systems so foundational that everything else gets designed around them.

### Games that found themselves late

Several well-known games show how far the final shape can drift from the start. Arvi Teikari recounts that Noita spent 2012 to 2016 cycling through an arena platformer, a Terraria-like survival game, a god game, a space RTS, a sci-fi explorer and a post-apocalyptic open world, starting from Petri Purho's blood-swimming puzzle platformer, before drifting into a roguelite as each concept ran into design problems ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 8:39](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=519)). Dwarf Fortress began as a planned two-month side project; the Adams brothers switched to real time to fix a mining colony's problems and to dwarves because dwarves mine, and because ideas got implemented so quickly in ASCII rather than 3D, it absorbed the persistent-world goals of Armok ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 14:37](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=877)). David Brevik held out for turn-based Diablo against Blizzard's repeated requests until a vote of about fifteen to seventeen staff in the kitchen went against him, with only about four wanting to stay turn-based; once he tried real time he knew it was right ([David Brevik 2023, 8:49](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=529)). His lesson is to keep a vision but not be rigid: listen to trusted feedback and expect the final game to differ from what you imagined ([David Brevik 2023, 28:53](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1733)).

### Fun is not the only criterion

Xalavier Nelson Jr. challenges the assumption that finding the fun settles every question. Followed uncritically, it becomes following a chain of beliefs and implications rather than deciding on them; if the most fun option creates something you could not justify or do not want to bring into existence, a suboptimal design decision is not just valid but important ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 10:49](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=649)). His team's practice is an audit: go through every category, number and value in the game and draw out its social, moral, cultural and physical implications, checking whether you can stand by each. He cautions that it can be bad faith to do this to other developers who may have had little agency, but for his own team it became both a necessity and a chance to say intentional things ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 20:00](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1200)).

Some checks are best run mid-development rather than at the start. Ezra Szanton uses synergy networks as a checkpoint on whether drafting feels the way he wants, adding or weakening synergies when it fails, and notes that building natural multiplicative mechanics in early, as Mr. Magpie's multiplier-and-money mechanic does, is an easy way to seed synergies players understand ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 29:11](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1751)).

**In practice.** Decide early: the core verb or mechanic in one sentence, or the feeling you want and one scenario that delivers it; any resource system that spells, items and skills will be built around; and the few guidelines (and values) you will not trade away. Leave to discovery: pacing, the map, secondary item types, and theme if the mechanic does not depend on it. Prototype the seed before anything else, and be ready for the game to become something else ([Josh Ge 2018, 5:50](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=350); [Dylan White 2021, 2:31](https://youtu.be/kvgKKRLil_8?t=151); [Casey Yano 2022, 11:04](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=664); [David Brevik 2023, 28:53](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1733)).

## Prototyping cheaply and throwing work away

Once you know what to test, test it as cheaply as possible. The talks give a toolbox of cheap media and, more importantly, an attitude: the prototype exists to answer a question and then be thrown away. They also give the strongest objection to that attitude, from someone who saw the prototype survive ([David Brevik 2023, 10:06](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=606); [Brian Cronin 2021, 5:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=305)).

### Cheap media

The cheapest prototype often never touches a game engine. Tyler Robertson calls spreadsheets a poor engine for shipping games but a fun, fast way to find out whether an idea is fun before moving to Unity or Unreal ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 2:00](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=120)). Once he had worked out reusable building blocks he built all the games in his talk in about a week, though discovering his advanced button technique had taken a year ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 14:57](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=897)). Brian Cronin laid out his dice roguelike's card ideas in a spreadsheet and built a Tabletop Simulator version before firing up Unity; friends' feedback was not glowing, but getting it that early shaped the game ([Brian Cronin 2025, 1:48](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=108)). David Dunham prototyped card-based resolution systems on paper, using plastic sleeves stiffened with bulk Magic cards so he could slip in any piece of paper ([David Dunham 2026, 8:43](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=523)).

When the question needs code, keep the code small. Brevik built the real-time Diablo prototype in a Friday afternoon, six to eight hours, after sending everyone home; had it failed, it would not have been a big waste. He still prototypes constantly and shelves what doesn't work ([David Brevik 2023, 10:06](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=606)). Max Hawkins, choosing which parts of his life to randomise, picked whatever was easy to build so he could get experience fast, using "can I do that in a day" as his constraint ([Max Hawkins 2019, 29:02](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=1742)).

### The disposable attitude

The talks converge on treating prototype work as something to delete without regret. Yano wrote Slay the Spire as decoupled code he was not afraid to delete: nothing relied on anything else, and if something did he removed it, so systems came and went within a week. He fixed code quality only when content work exposed problems, and admits this does not suit teams larger than two. He also advises naming functions after real game concepts (an elite room) rather than vague ones (a strong monster) ([Casey Yano 2022, 12:00](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=720)). The design side matched: Mega Crit would try a new feature, such as an enemy that eats your cards, for a single run and axe it on gut feeling if it didn't seem to work, with the two founders acting as harsh editors of each other's ideas, something Yano credits to years of friendship and critiquing games together ([Casey Yano 2022, 14:48](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=888)). Cutting is normal even for features that sound great: an early Caves of Qud echolocation mutation, with sonar bouncing off walls and a sonar attack, was one of the first mutations cut because it did not work well ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 12:09](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=729)).

Test the roughest version you can. Shawn Main's advice for a strong core mechanic with many possible secondary loops is to playtest early in the roughest possible shape and watch what testers find fun, which also teaches you how to layer systems ([Shawn Main 2021, 28:05](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1685)).

Cheap prototyping also keeps improbable ideas alive. Josh Grams encourages prototyping ideas that have been brewing for a while: the worst case is learning they have no legs, the best is something really cool ([Josh Grams 2020, 8:01](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=481)). Stray Fawn makes it routine. Every Monday and Friday afternoon is a "do what you want" prototyping session; Philomena Schwab's co-founder built the claw-machine prototype for Dungeon Clawler alone in one, the team moved on and left it in the freezer, and a later trip revived it ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 4:09](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=249)).

### When the prototype refuses to die

Cronin's warning cuts against all of this: the prototype will become the product. Monster Train's prototype was real-time, with three lanes, energy ticking up and combat at fixed rates. The team moved to turn-based play but kept building on much of the prototype code, which caused many problems ([Brian Cronin 2021, 5:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=305)). Years later he draws the boundary explicitly. Throwaway prototypes and game jams don't need careful gameplay architecture, but even smallish roguelikes on multi-month schedules benefit from planning it ([Brian Cronin 2024, 4:57](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=297)).

> A lot of the code that drives this prototype exists in the final version, so we just kept building on top of what we created. — [Brian Cronin 2021, 5:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=305)

Yano and Cronin are not really in conflict; they describe different moments. Yano's code was disposable while the design was still moving, in a team of two. Cronin's problem began when disposable code was carried into production. The risk is not prototyping in code but forgetting to decide when the prototype has ended ([Casey Yano 2022, 12:00](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=720); [Brian Cronin 2024, 4:57](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=297)).

There is also a motivation cost in what you prototype. Thomas Robertson describes how the drudgery of building UI during rapid prototyping eats time, forces you to budget more for it whether you like it or not, and saps creativity and motivation, which led him to experiment with variables that draw themselves ([Thomas Robertson et al. 2017, 1:08](https://youtu.be/H6fPIhLoA1Y?t=68)). Prototype media that skip UI (spreadsheets, paper, Tabletop Simulator) avoid that cost entirely.

**In practice.** Prototype in the cheapest medium that answers the question: a spreadsheet for numbers and card pools, paper or Tabletop Simulator for card and dice resolution, a day of code for feel and timing. Give an idea one run, an afternoon or a day; if it doesn't show promise, shelve it rather than delete the record of it. Keep prototype code decoupled while the design moves. When the game's direction is settled and the schedule runs to months, stop, decide which prototype code survives, and plan the architecture deliberately ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 2:00](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=120); [David Brevik 2023, 10:06](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=606); [Philomena Schwab 2024, 4:09](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=249); [Brian Cronin 2024, 4:57](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=297)).

## Where ideas come from: ideation, borrowing and lenses

Prototypes need ideas to test, and the talks treat producing them as a craft with techniques rather than as waiting for inspiration.

### Ideation is a skill

Marlowe Dobbe makes the case directly. Ideas are not magical things that appear from thin air; generating them is a skill you can practise. Sitting down to design fifty monsters from scratch would be nearly impossible for most people, so professionals rely on repeatable techniques; her three are the list of ten, referencing the game's mechanics, and visual reference ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 2:59](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=179)). The techniques can be mixed (she often combines a list of ten with mechanics or reference material), and the generation phase should stay playful and loose rather than chase the perfect idea each time ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 25:08](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=1508)). The output is a swarm, not a finished piece: concept sketches should be quick and rough enough to convey the vibe for a yes or no from the team, with little time per idea, from which you pick finalists or mash two together ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 19:20](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=1160)).

The same generate-wide-then-filter pattern appears in other forms:

- **Boon storms.** Alice Lai describes how Supergiant brainstormed Hades' boons in a spreadsheet, listing every association with a god for each ability slot (for Dionysus, everything from bacchanals to satyrs to wine), then filtered down to a strong core identity plus flourishes. Poseidon's core is knockback, but a narrative joke about him giving you things found in his couch became a side branch that grants random items ([Alice Lai 2021, 26:29](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1589)). Ideas were rated on both coolness and fit with Hades' fast play; a self-freezing invulnerability block was shelved because it would stun the player, and a repeatedly attempted active parry kept failing. Shelved ideas are revisited later ([Alice Lai 2021, 24:01](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1441)).
- **Theory grids.** Alexandra Leonhart lays out a grid of theorists and concepts against roguelike conventions, looks for "bright sparks" where they resonate, and filters the results through a genre or setting; her first test prototype is a cyberpunk roguelike drawing on Frankenstein, Patchwork Girl, Haraway's cyborg manifesto and Mark Fisher ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:24:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30294)). She argues that any lens that excites you, not only the queer theory she uses, can seed a design philosophy, and closes by asking designers "how are you queering your designs?", meaning which intersections they draw from ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:28:56](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30536)).
- **Ideation decks.** Tyler Coleman proposes a deck of ideation cards for roguelikes that pairs external data sources with game outputs, to push past obvious combinations. He usually starts from the output and looks for a data set, and forces himself towards weirder inputs (Van Gogh's face as a planet rather than rough rock) to test whether the algorithm and the source hold up ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:42:05](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=20525)).
- **Community jams.** Botnik produces pieces through writing jams in which around three hundred writers generate lines with a shared keyboard and vote on them, and an editor arranges the best into a script; the roguelike titles and tips in their show were made this way ([Botnik 2017, 3:55](https://youtu.be/IujSOW1OMWk?t=235)).
- **An LLM as improv partner.** Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster of Hidden Door compare working with an LLM to improv: impose too little and it becomes incoherent, but it needs room to roam, so "yes, and" its ideas and tie them to written trope threads ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 25:27](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1527)). Over a year their game moved from almost entirely order to almost entirely chaos and then to a mixed blend; their summary is composable blocks of chaos within order, simple solutions, fast iteration, and handling ethics at the start ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 29:52](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1792)).

### Borrowing is the genre's method

The second source of ideas is other games, and the talks are unembarrassed about it. Colin Liotta argues that it is fine to take something someone else built and improve it or take it somewhere new, and that this iterative borrowing is the premise of roguelikes ([Colin Liotta 2018, 5:35](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=335)). Tabea Iseli made it a ratio for Grimoire Groves: roughly 70% proven mechanics from roguelike crawlers and farming sims (home base, procedural levels, returning home on failure), 20% adaptations of familiar elements such as a non-violent take on combat, and 10% experiment, because players like games familiar to what they love and building on others' work is easier ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 5:23](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=323)). Coleman extends the idea to a series. In The Sims the previous game becomes the familiar base: the plumbob stays while the neighbourhood changes, and a breakout element like the Goth family, itself built on an Addams Family trope, becomes part of the familiar ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 17:19](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1039)).

Borrowing is a choice and can fail. Tyriq Plummer found Spelunky's single attack too straightforward and drew Catacomb Kids' combat from Smash Bros. instead; he also tried a hunger mechanic that didn't work, and sees no problem with that, because failure becomes obvious and your preferences steer you towards something enjoyable ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 30:30](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1830)).

The usual fear is that influence kills originality. Michael Brough argues the opposite: go back to the sources of the works you love, because you can only see what a creator added if you know what they drew from, and the deeper you go into the roots the more original your own transformations become. He points to Vance, Leiber, Lovecraft and Zelazny from Gygax's Appendix N list ([Michael Brough 2025, 47:40](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2860)). Paul Dean adds that studying how other works are made (films, novels, music, games) matters as much as studying the results, because creative problem-solving mirrors across media; he treated Vonnegut's drafts of Slaughterhouse-Five as being as valuable as the book ([Paul Dean 2025, 13:15](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=795)).

### Ideas from what is at hand

Many ideas in the talks grew from something already in front of the designer. Nick Bush's Word Processor began from the image of redacted documents and came together once he realised document navigation is an established set of movement mechanics people use every day ([Nick Bush 2026, 43:53](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=2633)). Bjarke Alexander Larsen needed something for players to do while the train in Telegrams from the Quiet Train spends real days travelling; he already had a database of people and addresses for the shipping system and turned it into a logic puzzle ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 2:27](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=147)). Younès Rabii saw masks in Tea Garden's generated flowers and added an interaction to wear them, a loop in which interpretations inspire interactions that inspire new interpretations ([Younès Rabii 2020, 6:59](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=419)). Nat Alison constructs hand-made sudoku by asking what happens if two constraint types combine, then turning the resulting break-in into themed deductions; sometimes something breaks and that logic is itself worth showing ([Nat Alison 2023, 13:15](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=795)).

Two process points help ideas come. Jon Perry found making UFO 50 as a fifty-game collection freeing because no single game had to carry the whole thing, so each could be experimental; he is unsure how to keep that freedom in a single project ([Jon Perry 2025, 39:00](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=2340)). And you need not start at the start: Dean wrote item descriptions for Pacific Drive in a random place and redrafted them as mechanics changed, and argues that insisting on beginning at the beginning is where people get stuck ([Paul Dean 2025, 9:31](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=571)).

**In practice.** To generate: write a list of ten; list every association with a theme per slot; cross a set of ideas you care about against the genre's conventions; pair an unexpected data source with an output; look at what your game already has (its data, its generated artefacts, an everyday interface) for a mechanic in waiting. To filter: rate each idea on coolness and on fit with the core play, keep a rough sketch rather than a finished piece, shelve rather than delete, and keep most of the game familiar so the new part stands out ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 2:59](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=179); [Alice Lai 2021, 24:01](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1441); [Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:24:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30294); [Tabea Iseli 2022, 5:23](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=323)).

## Deciding what to build: scope, cuts and productive constraints

Ideas are cheap; implementing them is not. The talks on scope converge on one rule and a handful of questions to enforce it.

### Hold to the core

Matt Ritchie, who calls scope his nemesis, states the rule: in a large project, always adhere to the core of the game and cut anything that doesn't add to it ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 4:48](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=288)). Eric Billingsley, who built a roguelike on the tiny Pico-8 platform, turns it into questions to ask of every system:

- **Do you really need it?** Ask especially if it is a genre staple, since designers assume staples are required without examining them ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 11:06](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=666)).
- **Is it worth the development time?** You have limited time and may not want to spend two years on a roguelike ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 11:06](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=666)).
- **Does it take attention away from the core?** Even a system that adds something can distract ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 12:11](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=731)).
- **Would leaving it out make the game more distinctive?** Think through which decisions its absence would force; some are compromises, some open possibilities you wouldn't otherwise find ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 12:11](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=731)).
- **Can one system do the job of another?** A merged system may be easier to build and easier to understand, since players transfer what they know from one context to another; if two systems don't quite merge, consider adjusting your goals or one system so it mostly covers the other ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 16:44](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1004)).

Against the Storm adds a roguelike-specific filter. Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński say they measured almost every feature by whether it made runs differ from each other, and in most cases declined features that didn't, even fantastic ones ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 7:51](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=471)).

### Scope as a design decision

Choosing what kind of game to make is the biggest scoping decision. Teikari explains that Noita chose a roguelite over an open world partly because the roguelite had a far more manageable scope, after years without a clear idea of how big the game was; the term "open world" itself implied size ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 12:01](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=721)). The choice removed whole problem areas: only one character's movement needed solving, and player-controlled AI agents, base building and pixel-precise digging went away ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 27:19](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1639)). Thomas Biskup scoped Ultimate ADOM's first release to a single dungeon crawl with four strongly differentiated races, because replicating all of ADOM plus a surface world would mean shipping in 2036 and starting with fifteen races and twenty classes could not be finished in time ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 5:53](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=353)).

Presentation is a scope choice too. Todd Furmanski presents his games as clicked still images rather than real-time animation so he can skip character animation and 60 FPS performance tuning: he did not want to spend three weeks teaching a character to lean over and pick up an object when text can say so. He points out that Myst was made by two people ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 4:53](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=293)). Stray Fawn chose deliberately basic art for Dungeon Clawler so a team of two or three, with an artist working one day a week, could iterate and add content fast; the demo took three to four months, against four years and thirteen people for The Wandering Village ([Philomena Schwab 2024, 6:11](https://youtu.be/MTam5RT8Kn0?t=371)).

### What expansion costs

Systemic games get more expensive to extend as they grow. Lai relays Supergiant programming lead Gavin's house-of-cards analogy from Hades: build the base wide early, because everything added later builds towards the fragile top, and entropy always wins. New effects that should work in a vacuum keep breaking existing systems; an ability that cleared a debuff for bonus damage forced a rework of a debuff system that had never anticipated conditional clearing ([Alice Lai 2021, 19:22](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1162)). Teikari says open-world ambitions on top of Noita's emergent simulation made the workload grow exponentially. The abandoned sword-casting blacksmith, where you dig a sword-shaped hole and pour molten metal into it, foundered because even digging one-pixel holes in a fully simulated world without it being annoying was a huge hassle ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 20:56](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1256)). Nathan Savant, who worked on the Nemesis system, says NPC reactivity can be stacked endlessly up to something that elaborate; the hard part is holding back and building only what you need ([Nathan Savant 2026, 13:32](https://youtu.be/rmddpcmIJ2I?t=812)).

### Keeping ambition cheaply

Cutting is not the only option. The talks offer ways to keep an ambitious feature while capping its cost.

**Build in an escape hatch.** Tarn Adams designs Dwarf Fortress's clue-based villain investigation so that if it fails it can collapse to someone saying "the bandits did it" and the rest of the arc still works. Think about the whole experience you want, and focus on the parts you feel you can do well ([Tarn Adams 2018, 20:43](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1243)).

**Price what a cut costs the player.** Alexei Pepers notes that closing off an edge case saves development time but turns a fuzzy boundary into a hard one and kills player suspense; on Blaseball, the vocabulary of system suspense helped explain that trade-off to engineers whose instinct was to cut fringe cases such as idolising dead players ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 34:38](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2078)). The cheaper alternative is to limit how often players can test a hypothesis. The Blaseball team mapped edge cases into an outcome tree and allowed an idol choice to trigger only twice; players who never see the exhaustive list cannot spot functionally identical outcomes behind different text, so unique work can be spent only on the branches players are likely to reach ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 36:38](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2198)).

**Judge content against its purpose.** Kristen Yu evaluates each piece of quest content against its stated purpose and tweaks it, cuts it or moves it to another bucket if it isn't serving it. The definitions can encode production limits such as "no cutscenes", which stop designers getting carried away ([Kristen Yu 2021, 17:55](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=1075)). At Improbable, where anyone could pitch quests, a proposed multiplayer quest was reclassified as single-player because it matched that purpose better ([Kristen Yu 2021, 19:13](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=1153)).

### The counter-position: the city, not the resort

Not everyone wants a tight game. George Moromisato's advice from NetHack is to "build a city instead of a resort": AAA games are resorts where you know what will happen, while NetHack accretes mismatched content over decades, a quantum mechanic fighting a vampire, into something living. He notes it takes decades, and he plans to work on Transcendence for the rest of his life ([George Moromisato 2016, 26:49](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1609)). Even the city has zoning: a NetHack developer coded a Jedi class with a battery-powered lightsaber, and the others cut it because it didn't fit, though Moromisato is unsure that was right ([George Moromisato 2016, 24:41](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1481)). Julian Day runs Shadow of the Worm as a test bed and zen garden in the ADOM and NetHack style, adding features like alcohol poisoning with little gameplay outcome; he admits this is to the game's detriment and that it is explicitly not a tight Crawl-style design ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 19:03](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=1143)).

The choice depends on time horizon and purpose. Ritchie, Billingsley and Against the Storm are trying to ship a coherent game on a budget; Moromisato and Day are describing lifelong projects whose value is in their accumulation. If you are not prepared to work on the game for decades, the city is not an option ([George Moromisato 2016, 26:49](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1609); [Darren Grey et al. 2020, 19:03](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=1143)).

### Constraints as a scope tool

Hard limits do the cutting for you. Furmanski calls roguelikes very susceptible to feature creep and found the Atari 2600's ROM, RAM and cycle limits an elegant cure, because running out forces you to stop and decide ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 3:06](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=186)). He now uses a minimal 2600 roguelike as his "hello world" for new platforms, porting it to the Atari 7800, Game Boy and Apple IIe, developing mostly in emulators with a BASIC-like language and testing on hardware through an SD cartridge ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 11:21](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=681)). On Pico-8, Billingsley found the code-size limit the hardest constraint, because unlike a sprite budget (a quarter of the sheet at 8x8 with four frames gives sixteen enemies) you cannot easily estimate how many lines pathing will take; halfway through, every new feature meant reworking existing code to fit, which he found frustrating but satisfying ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 5:41](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=341)). Lee Tusman points to Rogue 280, a roguelike in 280 characters with an @, HP, level, stairs and invisible monsters, as proof that extreme constraints let you build something quickly that still delights and plays with procedural generation ([Lee Tusman 2020, 6:47](https://youtu.be/-e4gF_SKWPk?t=407)).

Small platforms can also be a deliberate long-term choice. Eiríkr Åsheim describes Uxn, a permacomputing platform meant to keep old devices useful, conserve energy and minimise complexity, which runs on 20–30-year-old hardware and in modern browsers ([Eiríkr Åsheim 2024, 4:48](https://youtu.be/qogCwa12jEg?t=288)), and asks developers to consider whether a smaller, simpler, cozier environment is adequate for their roguelike, since it is easier to understand and reimplement than a big language or console ([Eiríkr Åsheim 2024, 10:25](https://youtu.be/qogCwa12jEg?t=625)). An old engine can free attention for content: Cara Esten Hurtle relays John Romero's account that building the Sigil Doom maps in an old engine let him think about the world rather than technical implementation ([Cara Esten Hurtle 2022, 5:29](https://youtu.be/ua2Brr6KCJM?t=329)). And reach can come cheaply: Chris McCormick wraps browser roguelikes in a web view, Apache Cordova for Android and Electron for desktop, so debug and shipping code are identical; the Android build of Asteroid took about a day ([Chris McCormick 2021, 24:39](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1479)).

**In practice.** Ask of every planned system: do I need it even though the genre expects it; is it worth the time; does it pull attention from the core; would its absence make the game more distinctive; can another system do its job; does it make runs differ? For an ambitious feature, design a simple fallback it can collapse to, and decide which edge cases you will close and what suspense that costs. Choose the game's form (roguelite over open world, still images over animation, basic art) to remove whole problem areas. If you can, pick a platform or a rule whose limits will stop you for you ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 11:06](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=666); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 7:51](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=471); [Tarn Adams 2018, 20:43](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1243); [Alexei Pepers 2025, 34:38](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2078); [Todd Furmanski 2019, 3:06](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=186)).

## Estimating time and money, and why it is always more

The production stories in these talks share a shape: the work took longer, and sometimes cost more, than planned. The useful question is not whether your estimate is wrong but how to correct for it.

### Think in curves

Tyler Coleman's diagnosis is that developers think linearly, one turn or one level at a time, but games and reality are distributed along curves with non-uniform contributions. He offers the 80/20 rule as a loose heuristic, not numerology (90/10 works as well); the point is that outcomes are rarely linear ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 5:25](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=325)). Applied to schedules, the rule recurses: 80% of the work takes 20% of the time, and that repeats at each stage of done, really done, integrated and polished. A one-week prototype takes four more weeks to finish, twenty more to be really done, and integration into a cohesive whole stretches it to about 125 weeks, and it is still not finished. His rule: multiply any estimate by four, then do it again ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 10:37](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=637)).

> Just always assume it'll take longer than you think; take that number, multiply it by four, then do it again. — [Tyler Coleman 2024, 10:37](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=637)

Coleman learned it on his own Merchant sequel. Adding "just multiplayer" to an existing game turned a one-year project announced for 2021 into a 2024 release, as the team realised how much more was needed to make it good; his takeaway is never to put a release year on a trailer ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 2:34](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=154)).

### The cases converge

Money follows time. Biskup says ADOM's revival consumed more than three times the $90,000 raised by crowdfunding, over a quarter of a million dollars; the crowdfunding money ran out in early 2015, he funded the project privately until the Steam release saved it, and even then the team could not pay everyone full-time though most worked full-time. He urges careful, realistic estimates ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 30:52](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1852)).

The other cases tell the same story at every scale:

- **ADOM.** In summer 1995, at 15,000 lines of C, Biskup told friends a couple more months would finish it; by 2016 it had over 230,000 lines and he says it will never be finished ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 5:15](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=315)). Version 0.9.9, when he thought it almost done, came more than four years and about seventeen releases before 1.0 in August 2001; version numbers, he notes, come to feel more meaningful than they are ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 13:38](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=818)).
- **Cogmind.** Josh Ge expected turning his 7DRL into a small commercial game to take a year; three and a half years later he was approaching 6,000 hours. Players liked early versions, he saw potential for more, and he wanted an impressive first commercial game because failure would mean giving up full-time development ([Josh Ge 2016, 14:20](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=860)).
- **Axu.** Ritchie's world map is a 200 by 200 grid of tiles, each of which opens into a 45 by 30 local map; he cites that scale as why the part-time project had taken four years and was about sixty percent done ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 2:24](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=144)).
- **Alphaman.** Jeff Olson's advice includes expecting the last 10% to take as long as the first 90%; finishing a complex game is like completing a PhD thesis, full of loose ends ([Jeff Olson 2023, 20:52](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=1252)).
- **Liotta's puzzle.** Liotta expanded his Mystery Hunt puzzle into a standalone app with about 120 levels, six dungeons and new mechanics such as ice, trailing lava and burning ice, and concluded that roguelikes are never finished ([Colin Liotta 2018, 15:54](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=954)).

Some of this growth comes from success: the game was going well, so it grew. Ge's players liked early Cogmind and he saw potential for more; Liotta expanded a single puzzle into a standalone app ([Josh Ge 2016, 14:20](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=860); [Colin Liotta 2018, 15:54](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=954)). Growth is not always a failure of planning, but it should be a decision, not a drift.

### What a tight schedule costs

Overruns also shape the game. Cronin says Monster Train had many small refactors, but the schedule eventually ruled out big ones, and the architecture probably limited which cards the team could make, a trade-off he considers unavoidable ([Brian Cronin 2021, 25:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1506)). Some problems simply take years: Iseli says that after two years, making a satisfying non-action loop was still one of Grimoire Groves' biggest challenges, in a project the team always knew was a big experiment ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 29:02](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=1742)). If the core of your game is experimental, budget for it staying unsolved for a long time.

Olson frames the long tail in a way that makes it bearable: if you make games for your own enjoyment your time is never wasted, so try something nobody has done, use as many playtesters as you can and embrace their criticism ([Jeff Olson 2023, 20:52](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=1252)).

**In practice.** Estimate, then multiply by four, then again, and treat the result as the more likely figure. Budget money for the multiplied schedule, not the first one, and know where funding comes from if it runs out. Treat "just" (just multiplayer, just one more system, just the last 10%) as a warning word. Do not announce a release year until the game is nearly done, and do not let version numbers stand in for progress. Decide early which architecture changes you will be able to afford late, because near the end of the schedule you may not ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 10:37](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=637); [Tyler Coleman 2024, 2:34](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=154); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 30:52](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1852); [Thomas Biskup 2016, 13:38](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=818); [Brian Cronin 2021, 25:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1506)).

## What procedural content really costs to produce

One line item deserves the multiplied estimate more than most. A common reason to reach for procedural generation (content made by algorithm rather than by hand, often shortened to procgen) is that it looks like the cheap way to get a lot of game. The talks that have actually shipped generated content say otherwise: generation moves the cost around, and often adds to it ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 30:06](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1806); [Leigh Alexander 2023, 27:41](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1661)).

### Generation is not a shortcut

Several independent talks converge on this. Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner, summing up how Wildermyth makes its generated heroes feel authored, list what it took: many traits per hero, traits shown visually, consistent voices, and handcrafted stories selected by trait with added acknowledgement of who the hero is. Belanger calls it a lot of work, and warns that the time it takes to hone a generator into something of high quality has to be weighed when you decide to use one at all ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 30:06](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1806)). Leigh Alexander makes the same point about writing: working in a generative mode is not labour-saving, and breaking text into components that recombine well can be harder and more complex than writing linear prose. Her reason for doing it anyway is that it is fun, not that it is cheap ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 27:41](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1661)).

The cost compounds downstream. Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang, describing the localisation of Caves of Qud, conclude that a procedural game does not just need a strong translator for each language; it needs a strong technical team for each language, because every language needs its own custom text processors and most of that work does not carry over to the next. Authorship itself becomes technical, with translators and English writers spending much of their time in raw text editors, and making procedural templates easy to author is still an open problem for them. New DLC strings arriving while a language is only 70% done is, for a part-time team of six to a dozen, a large production problem in itself ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:56:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6982)). Kingdom of Loathing shows the simpler version of the same trap: Zack Johnson says it is effectively unlocalisable, partly because its text is embedded in old PHP files and partly because so much of its humour is wordplay ([Zack Johnson 2016, 22:42](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=1362)).

> Procedural systems in general not only need a very complex and powerful translation. They need a very complex and powerful technical team. — [Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:56:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6982)

None of this means procgen is a bad bet for a small team. Gabriel Koenig, who usually works alone without a budget, turned to it precisely to make games bigger than he could build by hand ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 1:03](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=63)). The two positions are compatible: generation buys scale that a solo developer could not otherwise have, but the scale is not free, and the work of making it good, and of carrying it into other languages and other team members' hands, has to be in the budget from the start.

### Validating content that is chosen at runtime

Jurie Horneman gives the most usable framework for that budget. He separates *dynamic content selection* (picking barks, storylets or rooms from a pool at runtime) from seeded generation, and argues it must be validated differently from static content. The questions are the same two you ask of any content, whether it can break the game and whether it is good, but you answer them differently: with a pool, quality is easier to ship unevenly and harder to define ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 1:49](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=109)). His single closing takeaway is to explicitly budget time to work out how you will answer both questions, because that is real, skilled work ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 22:48](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1368)).

Two production details from Horneman matter for scheduling. First, the analysis sometimes cannot start until the content data is nearly complete: on one location-based project the team knew about a problem but could not choose a fix until the world, locations and quests were set up, and in the end they eyeballed quality rather than automating the check, which he counts as a risk ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 21:49](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1309)). Plan for some validation to land late, and do not assume a known risk can be closed early. Second, dynamic selection has a real production benefit: tag-based room selection decouples level creation from room creation, so different people can build levels and rooms in parallel without waiting on each other. Horneman notes that the same decoupling raises integration risk, which is exactly why the validation work matters ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 3:47](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=227)).

### Deciding what to generate

The talks offer several rules for spending procgen effort where it pays.

- **Weigh complexity against player impact.** Sébastien Benard, working solo after Dead Cells, decides what to proceduralise by comparing a feature's implementation complexity with its effect on the player. His contrast: a random platform generator is very complex and has little impact, while well-dispatched randomised loot is easy to build and has a large one ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 33:10](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1990)).
- **Prefer a simple generator with good content.** Alexander Birke's summary from Sea Of Rifts is that a simple solution with good design and good content beats a clever algorithm, and that using existing tools helps a commercial game ship. His narrative designer already knew Tracery and Ink, and, as the session host added, nobody can be hired who already knows your custom system ([Alexander Birke 2024, 23:06](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=1386)).
- **Start with the dumbest version.** Darius Kazemi relays Brian Reynolds' account of AI in Rise of Nations, which started with a strategy picked at random and only grew more complex if playtests showed it was needed; Kazemi makes his own bots as stupid as possible until they amuse enough people ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 25:08](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1508)).
- **Curate at development time.** Mike Cook points out that the designer can choose which generated output ships. Elite shipped only a few of the galaxies its generator could produce, and Cook suggests that generated rule systems could likewise be picked by hand, one per monthly patch, because a system is impactful enough to justify that ([Mike Cook 2023, 23:13](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1393)).
- **Design where the content lives.** For location-based work, Emilia Lazer-Walker built a geofencing tool to walk the physical space, draw regions and tag them with seed words for her generator. Being on site was essential, and playtesting and walking the space took the bulk of the time; the edit-walk-test loop was slower than she wanted ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 17:54](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1074)). The general lesson is that the iteration loop of a generator includes wherever its output is experienced, and that loop has a cost.

### Two ways a generator eats a project

Pepers names the failure modes. The first is personal: watching a generator spin out content is so absorbing, like spinning straw into gold, that developers can lose days or years tinkering with it and forget the game they meant to make ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 3:56](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=236)). The second is organisational: planning and marketing need someone in the room who understands what procgen can and cannot do, or a team ends up promising thousands of unique NPCs to talk to while refusing to hire writers because an algorithm will handle it ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 21:49](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=1309)).

**In practice**, budget for these costs before committing to a generator:

- the time to hone output to the quality bar, not just to get it running ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 30:06](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1806));
- content written in components, which may take longer than linear content ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 27:41](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1661));
- per-language technical work if you will localise generated text ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:56:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6982));
- time to decide how you will check both "can it break?" and "is it good?", some of which can only happen once content is nearly complete ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 22:48](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1368); [Jurie Horneman 2023, 21:49](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1309));
- a check of each generated feature's player impact against its build cost ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 33:10](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1990));
- someone who can tell planning and marketing what the generator will really deliver ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 21:49](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=1309)).

## Playtesting as the centre of development

Everything so far assumes you can tell whether the game is working. The talks are clear that, on your own, you cannot.

### Why you cannot be your own tester

Cronin's argument is blunt: developers are bad at knowing whether their game is fun and bad at knowing whether it is understandable. He often finds that something he thought was clear confuses five testers in a row. So he rejects the traditional pipeline (idea, design document, prototype, production, QA, release) in favour of tight iteration loops built around playtests, and he treats developers who skipped playtesting and succeeded as likely survivorship bias ([Brian Cronin 2025, 7:40](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=460)).

> Devs are bad at knowing if their game is fun. Devs are bad at knowing if their game is understandable. — [Brian Cronin 2025, 7:40](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=460)

Yano adds a complementary point from Slay the Spire: developers should also play their own game a lot. Mega Crit played two or three runs a week, and the effect was that the team's conversation moved from talking about mechanics to talking about the possibility space, which they could then make real. Yano worries that the loop is harder to close in larger productions where designer, implementer and tester are separate roles ([Casey Yano 2022, 23:54](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=1434)). The two views fit together: playing your own game shows you what the game *could* be, and other people's play shows you what it actually is to someone who did not build it.

The cautionary cases agree. Zapata's Civilization-inspired Ruler had extensive infrastructure, with cities, roads and trade, but was not playtested until the very end and turned out broken: players could reach the space age very quickly. His lesson is to invest in playtesting and find friends or online contacts to help, because a developer needs someone else to test ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 12:46](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=766)). Sersa Victory's Rogue remake let players smash petrified out-of-depth monsters for experience at the risk of attracting a medusa; on paper it was a good risk-reward choice, but Discord players said they rarely did it because the reward did not justify the risk, so she retuned it ([Sersa Victory 2022, 24:48](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1488)). Nick McConnell, from maintaining Angband, says a developer needs a vision but should get it in front of players early, because grand plans often prove unpopular on release ([Nick McConnell 2021, 10:20](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=620)).

The genre's history points the same way. Glenn Wichman says Rogue's creators had a constant community of testers in the college computer lab who played each new feature as soon as it went in; he did not realise at the time how valuable that was, especially for a genre that is hard to test because circumstances rarely repeat ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 7:47](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=467)). Jeff Olson's Alphaman relied on two dedicated playtesters: Greg Krol, who tried every weird edge case (using a mental mutation on his own backpack) and probably crashed DOS several times, and Peter Jessop, who contributed many ideas ([Jeff Olson 2023, 19:05](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=1145)). The two roles, breaker and idea-giver, are still worth recruiting for.

Cronin also puts a number on what this costs. As a part-time solo developer he ran about 88 one-on-one, hour-long sessions over the project, 50 of them in the first year, all over Discord or Google Meet ([Brian Cronin 2025, 3:15](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=195)). He argues that small teams under-use this live form, often relying only on asynchronous testing where people play and send back notes; asynchronous testing has its place, but one-on-one synchronous sessions are the critical tool ([Brian Cronin 2025, 7:28](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=448)).

### Silent observation or active listening

The talks agree that you must watch people play. They disagree about whether to talk while you do.

Biskup's experience with ADOM is the strongest case for watching without explaining. After Steam feedback on the user interface, the team began putting people who had never played ADOM in front of a notebook and observing them; after the first 60-minute session he had about 150 notes, and he calls user testing their most important mechanism ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 38:51](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=2331)). Testing with diverse small groups (non-gamers, casual players, RPG players and roguelike players) with no explanation taught the team more in an hour than 20 years of ADOM had, and Biskup calls waiting that long a huge mistake: even finding the start button can be a challenge ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 19:09](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1149)). He adds two cautions. Designing for novices risks overcorrecting, so ideas are tested early and failures dropped (the UI had been reworked at least three times), and small test groups are themselves a bubble, so a larger test base is needed ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 26:55](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1615)). And the late game can only be balanced with feedback from core power players, the only ones who reach it, but their influence must be kept away from the early stages, where they would push premature optimisation because everything feels too easy to them ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 32:47](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1967)).

Dan DiIorio's rule from Luck be a Landlord is close to Biskup's: do not steer testers toward the right way to play. An early tester kept taking Coal, a symbol worth nothing that has a 2% chance per spin to become a five-coin diamond, and kept losing. Asked afterwards, the tester said that if it transformed they would be fine, a piece of player reasoning DiIorio says he would never have learned if he had stepped in ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 11:52](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=712)).

Cronin explicitly rejects total silence. He talks as an active listener and decides case by case: if a question bears on what is being tested, he asks "what does your intuition say?"; otherwise he answers and moves on. He unblocks testers stuck on bugs, takes notes audibly so they know their time is valued, and tries not to be so chatty that he biases them ([Brian Cronin 2025, 23:38](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1418)). The disagreement is narrower than it looks. Everyone agrees not to explain the game or correct the player's choices; the choice is whether to keep the session flowing with neutral questions. Silent observation suits interface and onboarding tests, where the question is what a stranger does alone; active listening suits remote sessions and design questions, where you need the player's reasoning, which DiIorio also had to ask for afterwards.

### Cronin's method

Cronin's talk is the most complete playtest procedure in the talks, and it is built for teams of one or two.

**The loop.** Form a hypothesis, run a round with one to five testers, synthesise the feedback into prioritised action items, act on them, and repeat. Focus each round on one hypothesis without ignoring the rest of the experience; it is not strict science. His example of the kind of result to expect is Resident Evil painting interactable objects yellow, plausibly after tests showed players missing them ([Brian Cronin 2025, 11:28](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=688)).

**What early tests validate.** Four things: whether the second-to-second play is fun, whether the minute-to-minute loop is fun, whether players understand what is happening, and whether the art and theme are compelling. In a deckbuilder, drawing and playing cards is the core nugget; adding cards, shopping and moving between battles is the outer loop. Prototypes can be paper or a mod of another game, and music and artwork can be tested too ([Brian Cronin 2025, 10:39](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=639)).

**How many testers.** Three to five per round is usually enough, because patterns repeat. Cronin takes the five-user figure from the book *Sprint*, and says he usually has a strong gut feeling by three, sometimes one. You do not need twenty people for every change ([Brian Cronin 2025, 13:16](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=796)).

**Finding and tracking testers.** Ask: friends and family, Discord servers, playtesting subreddits, social media, paid services, and above all referrals from testers. One Facebook post produced six or seven sessions. Do not over-rely on other game developers, who view games in a particular way, though trusted genre experts are useful ([Brian Cronin 2025, 18:47](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1127)). Track every session and every interested person in one place, with name, date, build, notes, status and how to reach them; this builds a bank of future testers and a history of the game you can look back on ([Brian Cronin 2025, 15:50](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=950)).

Subset Games makes the opposite choice for a specific reason. Justin Ma and Matthew Davis build the most hardcore version of a game first and make it approachable later, so their early testers are other developers and people who know their work, who can imagine the finished presentation and are not thrown by strange mechanics ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 8:14](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=494)). The choice of tester follows from what the build is: an unpolished, deliberately hard prototype needs testers who can see past it; a build meant to test comprehension needs people who cannot.

**Running the session.** Open by thanking the tester and asking warm-up questions about what they play, which gets them talking and reveals their perspective: one tester who had never played a turn-based game called Cronin's game "chill". Then ask explicitly for what they find fun, frustrating and confusing, and tell them they will not hurt your feelings ([Brian Cronin 2025, 21:12](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1272)). When players of a crunchy game go quiet, prompt with "What are you feeling now?", "What decision are you making?", "Do you know what to click next?" or "I sense you're a bit frustrated, I'm curious why"; Cronin keeps his webcam on and encourages testers to do the same so he can read their faces ([Brian Cronin 2025, 25:17](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1517)).
