**Not getting defensive.** If a tester is confused by a burning skeleton and you point at the status icon they missed, they will retreat to "the game was good, thanks". Use "I" language that owns the mistake ("I can see where I made a mistake") and write it down ([Brian Cronin 2025, 22:18](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1338)).

**Acting on it.** Do not try to act on everything. Mark action items in each session's notes, gather them with attribution into a prioritised list with hypothesis items first, and accept that unfixed issues will resurface or vanish with later changes. But do at least one thing per playtest; an hour of someone's time that changes nothing is wasted ([Brian Cronin 2025, 15:26](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=926)). Finally, interpret rather than obey. Cronin says there are no bad playtesters: a harsh tester outside the target audience can be partly right, while friendly one-on-one testers bias positive, which is why anonymous feedback from a public demo is also worth having ([Brian Cronin 2025, 29:34](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1774)).

### A compact playtest protocol

1. Write down the hypothesis for this round ([Brian Cronin 2025, 11:28](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=688)).
2. Recruit three to five testers who fit the question; log them ([Brian Cronin 2025, 13:16](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=796); [Brian Cronin 2025, 15:50](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=950)).
3. Warm up, then ask for fun, frustrating and confusing ([Brian Cronin 2025, 21:12](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1272)).
4. Do not explain the game or correct the player's choices; ask neutral questions when they go silent ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 11:52](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=712); [Brian Cronin 2025, 25:17](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1517)).
5. Own confusion as your mistake, out loud ([Brian Cronin 2025, 22:18](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1338)).
6. Turn notes into a prioritised list and ship at least one change before the next round ([Brian Cronin 2025, 15:26](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=926)).
7. Periodically test with people unlike your regulars, and keep power-player feedback out of early-game tuning ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 26:55](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1615); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 32:47](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1967)).

## Developing in public: community feedback, early access and update cadence

Once a game is in players' hands, through a public demo, early access or ongoing updates, feedback stops being something you schedule and becomes something that arrives constantly. The talks agree on two principles for handling it, and both are about the developer's discipline rather than the players': someone must triage it consistently ([Brian Cronin 2021, 18:11](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1091)), and the team, not the crowd, decides ([Chris King 2022, 10:09](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=609)).

### Feedback pays only if someone triages it

Cronin credits one tool, more than anything else, for Monster Train's success: consistently acting on feedback. The producer reviewed reports daily, filing them into Jira and tagging them in Slack with emoji reactions for "already filed" or "not a bug". It was a lot of work, and Cronin says it made the game what it is ([Brian Cronin 2021, 18:11](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1091)). The front end was just as deliberate. Pressing F8 in game sent a report straight to Slack with the log file, save file and a screenshot, with no username, password or alt-tabbing to a website. Even though battles were not resumable mid-fight, the save restored the start of the battle, and the logs revealed problems such as out-of-memory errors. The system is still in the Steam build ([Brian Cronin 2021, 16:25](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=985)).

> I think this tool more than anything was the reason for our success. — [Brian Cronin 2021, 18:11](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1091)

### Feedback is not a democracy

Chris King's framing is that the community is not voting. Every suggestion goes through the team's own taste, scope and sense of fit, and the team stays the final arbiter; popularity alone is not a reason to implement something. When the team declines a popular request it says so publicly, so the community knows it is being heard, and King notes that valuable ideas often come from one-off suggesters who are never heard from again ([Chris King 2022, 10:09](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=609)). He still values player input highly: he splits the feature pipeline into recognition (what needs changing), ideation (proposed changes), decision and implementation, and says choosing from a wide pool of player ideas gets him to implementation faster than inventing everything himself ([Chris King 2022, 2:26](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=146)).

Andrew Aversa gives the sharper version for difficulty in Tangledeep: listen to the problem players describe, not necessarily the fix they ask for. Veterans asked for more hotbars; Tangledeep instead limited hotbars, and nobody complained ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 17:23](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1043)). NetHack's DevTeam shows the same filter running over decades. Jesse Collet says the saying "the DevTeam thinks of everything" largely reflects the team absorbing what players tried and suggested, and credits it to those players; the team's process was to ask first whether an idea made sense, and then how to make it work ([Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 30:13](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=1813)).

### What players can see that you cannot

The case for developing in public is that players see things the developer has become blind to. King says that after two years of development you have no idea what your new-player experience is like, nor which flavour decisions clash with part of your audience ([Chris King 2022, 2:47](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=167)). But he also names the limit of a long early access: the committed community stops representing first-time players, and familiarity with regulars (one civil member who is always doom-laden, for instance) makes it hard to know what a newcomer would experience. Newcomer feedback has to come from elsewhere, such as convention demos; he calls this a tough, open question ([Chris King 2022, 15:10](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=910)).

Players are also the best stress-testers of a large possibility space. Lai says Hades relied heavily on its early access and speedrunning communities to find design holes where things became too powerful too quickly, such as a Dionysus and Athena pairing that cancelled any projectile ([Alice Lai 2021, 22:33](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1353)). Dylan Gedig lurks on Twitch while working on Peglin: streams show whether balance works, since players rarely take the path the designer thinks optimal, and with around 100 relics and 30 orbs a clip of a bug shows the whole loadout needed to reproduce it, which a text report often cannot ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 10:49](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=649)). Liotta, reflecting on the roguelike puzzle he built for the 2017 MIT Mystery Hunt, recommends releasing early and studying metrics from real players: early levels were hosted publicly, a few thousand people played, and seeing which levels they enjoyed, hated and got stuck on taught him quickly what made a good puzzle ([Colin Liotta 2018, 10:12](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=612)).

The warning cases are about developers who did not listen. Nicholas Feinberg recounts a Crawl player who reported that summoned ice beasts no longer did damage and was told that stuff happens; in fact a bug meant the elemental damage was printed but never applied, and the developers took a full year longer to notice than that player did ([Nicholas Feinberg 2020, 4:52](https://youtu.be/GMkBT4UbvAs?t=292)). A probability complaint is not always just bad luck.

Some teams bring players in even earlier. Iseli describes Grimoire Groves' participatory design: going to players as early as possible, within an indie budget, to ask what they wanted. Players chose the art direction and named the game, and their feedback moved the pitch from "Wizard of Legend meets Adventure Time" to "Hades or Cult of the Lamb meets Animal Crossing", serving a cozy audience the team felt was underserved ([Tabea Iseli 2024, 11:51](https://youtu.be/-MX1imoSxTg?t=711)).

### Data and experiments

Analytics help, but the Against the Storm team warns how they mislead in a roguelite. Pick rates reward the dull: a plain +50% woodcutting perk tops the charts, while the most interesting and best-loved perks are often situational and therefore rarely picked. The team, coming from mobile games, reviews anonymous gameplay data every two weeks but does not follow it blindly, and reads feedback on every channel alongside it ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 14:18](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=858)). For controversial changes they open an experimental beta branch to their most dedicated players and ask pointed questions, above all whether the change makes play more repetitive or more interesting. Ideas pass through the designer, then a team decision, then players, and many features went through three or four iterations before both developers and players were happy ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 12:17](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=737)). Data tells you what players do; a targeted beta question tells you whether it is any good.

### Update cadence

How often you ship shapes what you can design. Evan Debenham ships a Shattered Pixel Dungeon update every two to three months, each with one primary focus. Major updates used to take six months or more; now even big overarching work is split into two-to-three-month deliverables, which limits feature creep and keeps returning players finding something new, and he credits it for players who have stayed since 2014 ([Evan Debenham 2021, 6:54](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=414)). The shorter cycle also makes experiments cheap: if an update does not work, the worst case is about two months lost, and the next update can revisit it, which frequently happens ([Evan Debenham 2021, 7:34](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=454)). Every update gets an open public beta of at least a week, during which Debenham fixes critical issues (usually stable after a day), finishes content, makes feedback-driven tweaks and gives community translators time to work. He acknowledges the complaint that players should not be your QA, but argues it applies to big studios: for a small independent developer who is honest about it, early content in exchange for testing is a fair, symbiotic deal ([Evan Debenham 2021, 13:00](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=780)).

Blaseball is the extreme case. Joel Clark says the promise of weekly updates and continual change forced an improvisational design process with little filtering, because any heavier filter would leave no time to ship changes; the team works from the subconscious and accepts that the design is raw ([Joel Clark 2020, 10:48](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=648)). It also prioritises new over better: a steady stream of new systems keeps the game unpredictable and gives the community more to interpret, and partly the team simply cannot afford to tear down and rebuild a broken system when adding a simple new one is easier ([Joel Clark 2020, 14:24](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=864)). That is a choice for a live game built around surprise, not a general rule.

A roguelike's structure rewards growing in public. Peglin was scoped as a six-month project covering one area and only became a three-act game once it found traction; Gedig points out that new content in a roguelike enriches areas players replay constantly, and a basic feature such as viewing the full map was only prioritised because players asked ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 18:57](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1137)).

The counterweight is Dan DiIorio's warning: fix a design problem as soon as you see it, because changing beloved content gets harder the longer it ships. Luck be a Landlord's Cultist symbol, useless alone and stronger in numbers, pushes players into dull all-or-nothing builds; DiIorio noticed early but kept it because players liked it, and years after early access a change would provoke far more backlash ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 8:13](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=493)). Early access is when a change is cheapest; it is not a reason to defer one.

### When the bug is the feature

Jason Grinblat questions the assumption under all of this. Bug methodologies treat every bug as an interruption of an intended experience to be triaged and fixed; for games built as scaffolds for explorable worlds, where bugs come from systems colliding, he asks whether designers can make explicit room for bugs that enchant rather than only admiring them after the fact ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 4:07](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=247)). The constraint is labour. Turning a bug into a polished feature takes work, so a team can only do it for some bugs; for the rest it must either accept what is on screen or remove it if it is truly bad ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 26:43](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1603)). Add a third category to your triage, "keep and develop", and budget for it like any other feature.

**In practice:**

- Put a one-key report button in the game that attaches logs, save and screenshot, and route reports somewhere the team already looks ([Brian Cronin 2021, 16:25](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=985)).
- Assign one person to read and triage every report, daily if you can ([Brian Cronin 2021, 18:11](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1091)).
- Filter suggestions by your own taste and scope; when you say no to something popular, say so publicly ([Chris King 2022, 10:09](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=609)). Treat requests as descriptions of problems ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 17:23](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1043)).
- Read analytics alongside written feedback, and test contentious changes on an opt-in beta branch with specific questions ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 14:18](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=858); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 12:17](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=737)).
- Get newcomer feedback from outside your core community ([Chris King 2022, 15:10](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=910)).
- Pick a cadence you can keep with one focus per update and a public beta before each release ([Evan Debenham 2021, 6:54](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=414); [Evan Debenham 2021, 13:00](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=780)).
- Fix design problems while the audience is still small ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 8:13](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=493)).

## Teams, tools and pipelines

For a small team, a central production question is how quickly a piece of content can go from someone's head into the running game. The talks treat iteration speed as the goal that tools and team structure serve ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 3:51](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=231)), and then count the cost of the tools ([Spencer Egart 2021, 13:44](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=824)).

### Iteration speed as the goal

Birke states it as policy on Sea Of Rifts. As tech lead he aimed never to be an implementation or a decision bottleneck: tech must not block content, the decision maker must not block decisions, and anyone on the team should be able to push content into the game without checking first. Iteration speed is paramount, because without it you are in for a world of pain; he cites the book *Turn the Ship Around* as inspiration for letting people do their jobs ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 3:51](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=231)). The game is kept always playable with automated tests and frequent playtests, and artists and programmers share responsibility for both aesthetics and performance rather than splitting into those who care about looks and those who care about frame rate ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 5:15](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=315)). Opening tools to the whole team pays off in surprises: when he handed procedural tools to others, they used them in ways he did not anticipate, as when an artist ignored the coding rules of a sub-tiling shader and used offsets to make two stained-glass window types from one tile ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 23:16](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1396)).

Several developers converge on the same lesson from the code side: make adding content easy, and more content follows. Thomas Robertson says the most important thing he did on his procedural super attacks was set himself up for success; once new effect atoms were easy to add, he immediately made more. If adding a fire effect is hard you will not get around to it, and if it is easy you will add ice too ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 8:11](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=491)). Danny Day built Desktop Dungeons' event-listener system so balance changes would not mean searching a growing codebase; it delivered, letting him build two whole new classes for an update in a week, against months of slog updating the interface for mobile ([Danny Day 2018, 23:36](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1416)). Biskup reports the same effect from Ultimate ADOM's data-driven entity component system: the pentagram that let a character possess other bodies took about a day, but the soul-exchange spell that reused it took about eight minutes because of external configuration, and every new component suggests around twenty more items, spells or monsters that could reuse it ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 4:49](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=289)).

### What tools cost

The same architecture can be expensive. Biskup warns that a full entity component system (ECS, an architecture that builds game objects from data components rather than class hierarchies) is not trivial: Ultimate ADOM's took nine months with 10–15% still to do, and getting it to run at reasonable speed is part of the cost. He still recommends it for games that push the boundaries of interaction ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 37:44](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=2264)).

Tools can also be built at the wrong grain. Stav Hinenzon describes Sunshine Shuffle's dialogue tool, designed to be fully atomic: every node created and linked by hand. In practice the work consolidated into lines of dialogue and turns of poker, so the atomic graph only added time-consuming authoring work ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 9:09](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=549)). Her takeaways are to design tooling by talking with the people who will use it, and that flawed tools can still ship a game you are proud of ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 15:00](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=900)).

The decision rule comes from Spencer Egart: weigh time saved against time invested, and generally do not build tools during a game jam such as the 7DRL. His demo generator sits in a project named for the 2021 7DRL, for which he shipped no game. When a tool is meant to widen expressive range rather than save time, the value is harder to measure and becomes a judgment call ([Spencer Egart 2021, 13:44](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=824)). Patrick Kemp at Spry Fox shows how to keep the investment small. Tooling that pays off later in production is hard to justify against feature work, but an HTML page that parses the game's JSON was quick to build and new dashboard views take a day or two ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 27:46](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1666)). One view, not in the original spec and trivial to add, counts how often each dialogue animation tag is used, so writers can spot over- and under-used animations and animators can see what to make next ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 19:39](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1179)).

Birke's tools on Sea Of Rifts are about preventing errors and collisions. Custom Unity editors make data entry less error-prone than raw formats such as XML, because the tool shows the structure and enforces field types ([Alexander Birke 2024, 20:29](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=1229)). To avoid merge conflicts in a game built in a single Unity scene, the lead alone owns the canonical scene; everyone else works on a copy named after themselves, refreshed at intervals, with a console warning when it is out of date, and assets are split by discipline so the narrative designer's content lives in separate files and never touches prefabs ([Alexander Birke 2024, 21:08](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=1268)). Sofie Kjær Schmidt adds the same instinct for non-code tools: avoid juggling too many. She keeps overall art direction on a Miro board but moved per-environment style guides to Google Slides because they are easy to modify, share and print without account setup, and she drops any tool that causes friction ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 9:17](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=557)).

Sergio Garces gives the asset-side version for 3D on a budget: buy cheap store assets early so you prototype with something better than boxes, then shop for specific needs while bookmarking interesting finds, and expect to modify every asset, which needs at least some technical-art skill. If you cannot find what you need, you may have to change plans or build it ([Sergio Garces 2022, 26:22](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=1582)).

### People between disciplines

Tools only go so far if people cannot understand each other. Gillian Smith distinguishes additive interdisciplinarity (A plus B), multiplicative (expertise at the intersection) and integrative, which trains people to be translators between disciplines, a role she says interdisciplinary game teams badly need. Her example: a game-design and robotics team building a robot escape room spent about six months not realising that the y-axis points out of the screen in robotics software but up in 3D modelling software ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:20:26](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4826)). Pepers makes the procgen version: larger teams need procgen translators and advocates to bridge deep specialists and everyone else, while small teams can afford to be all specialists ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 28:13](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=1693)).

Shared vocabulary is the practical form of translation. Yu describes how agreeing on quest terminology at Improbable let designers hand programmers a complete list of every objective type they wanted, long shots included, so the quest system was built to support them all up front rather than broken by later requests ([Kristen Yu 2021, 8:32](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=512)).

Writing is the discipline most often missing. Julian Day observes that most roguelike teams are teams of one and most roguelike developers are not writers, so text gets treated as a chore before getting back to mechanics ([Julian Day 2020, 3:31](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=211)). Leigh Alexander's remedy is pairing: she asked Brian Bucklew to teach her spreadsheets as a generative back end, and suggests generative coders find a writer obsessed with some story domain they know nothing about ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 32:34](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1954)). Zapata gives the general rule for small teams: split work so each person does what they add most value to. On Fusion Abyss his partner wrote the 3D display code while he wrote an Ultima Underworld-style level generator; they struggled with graphics, and he advises getting an artist on board ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 19:47](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=1187)).

**In practice:**

- Build a tool when the time it saves clearly exceeds the time it costs; skip tools in a jam ([Spencer Egart 2021, 13:44](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=824)).
- Design the tool with the person who will use it, at the grain they actually work in ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 15:00](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=900); [Stav Hinenzon 2023, 9:09](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=549)).
- Start with the cheapest version, such as a web page over your existing data files ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 27:46](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1666)).
- Make adding one more piece of content trivial ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 8:11](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=491)).
- Let anyone push content without waiting on you, keep the build playable, and give each file one owner ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 3:51](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=231); [Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 5:15](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=315); [Alexander Birke 2024, 21:08](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=1268)).
- Agree on vocabulary before building systems that several disciplines feed ([Kristen Yu 2021, 8:32](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=512)).

## Keeping going: motivation, pace and the solo developer

Most roguelikes are made by one person or a few, often part-time, so the real constraint is rarely skill. It is sustaining effort for years.

### Know why, and add something every day

Ritchie starts with motive. Know why you are making the game (creativity, money, challenge, learning) and who it is for, and know why you abandoned past projects: he lists lack of time, lack of motivation, failed ideas and scope creep. His own drivers are creativity, challenge and learning, since donations earned about $400 in two years ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 4:06](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=246)). His own failures are instructive: projects that repeatedly changed genre (a survival game becoming a Binding of Isaac-like) and that depended on collaborating artists who never delivered ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 3:08](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=188)).

His working rule is to add something new every day you work on the game, however small; endless tweaking and premature optimisation produce no progress, and tweaked code will be replaced anyway. An hour a day, about the time spent watching television, makes a difference ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:26](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=326)). To keep that hour fresh, he rotates between art, system code and new content such as enemies ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 7:49](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=469)).

Daigle, writing for beginners, arrives at the same two ideas. What kept him going when he had repeatedly bounced off programming was small, highly visible progress; abstract problems are the hardest to stick with, and GameMaker helped by providing ready functions so his time went to the fun parts ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 12:35](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=755)). And some features, pathfinding for instance, are infinite problems that will always yield a little more progress, so learn when good enough is good enough and keep two or three features to rotate between, switching when one turns into a grind ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 13:26](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=806)). McConnell says the same from maintaining Angband: avoid rabbit holes, and sometimes you just need to do it and ship ([Nick McConnell 2021, 10:55](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=655)).

> You want to add something new every day that you're working on it, even if it's small. — [Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:26](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=326)

### Habits for learning while building

Daigle's other advice is aimed at people learning to program through their game. It is fine to change a variable, recompile and see what happens; experienced programmers call that bad practice, but for a beginner it is how you learn what functions do, and work that gets thrown away is fine because the point is understanding ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 14:23](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=863)). When stuck, explain the problem in full to a rubber duck or a non-technical friend, including every variable and every failed fix; organising it for someone else often surfaces the answer ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 25:15](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1515)). And track the licence and credit of every third-party asset from the first day, even while just goofing around, or months later you will not know where anything came from; OpenGameArt and Wikimedia Commons let you filter by licence ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 16:42](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1002)).

Many roguelikes start as learning projects. ADOM began in 1992 when Biskup wanted a project to learn C; he looked at the NetHack sources to modify them, found them too advanced, and took what he ironically calls the easier route of writing his own game ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 2:06](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=126)). Ian Bettencourt, at a 2016 lightning talk, described starting a roguelike in C before a college class with nothing but a compiler, a debugger and ncurses, writing his own engine, finding linked lists and arrays more useful than the trees his classes stressed, and learning to decouple code by showing it to his roommate ([Tariq et al. 2016, 20:49](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1249)). Kate Compton gives the attitude: aim for the 95% of the fun you can reach with 5% of the knowledge, taking what you need from computer science and getting back to your life ([Kate Compton 2020, 4:01](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=241)).

### Pace and burnout

Biskup's history with ADOM shows both ends of the pace problem. In 2010, close to burnout from juggling five or six projects alongside a PhD, he cut everything else and returned to ADOM because its players were still there after ten years ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 17:22](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1042)). Later, when an investor allowed the team to work on it full-time for the first time in 25 years, releases went from about one a quarter or a year to nine in six weeks ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 5:32](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=332)). His conclusion is that steadiness matters more than volume: even 20% of a full-time team's effort gives ADOM more steady development than years of hobby time worked only "when time allows and nobody is sick", enough for perhaps monthly releases ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 15:04](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=904)).

### Distance, backups and lowered stakes

Joel Ryan, who spent about five years on the Sil-Q tileset, describes two hazards of long creative work. Up close, you resist throwing away work you laboured over; stepping away for days or months erodes that resistance, and redesigned tiles almost always came back better. He had to discard all his early werewolf work, and likens it to dying in a roguelike: you are making yourself into the person who can make the thing ([Joel Ryan 2022, 26:16](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1576)). The opposite hazard is "noodling", too many small changes that slowly push the work in the wrong direction, like over-working clay on a wheel. Keep backups, compare against older versions, and sometimes pull the best part of an old version, a colour scheme or a good left leg, into the new one ([Joel Ryan 2022, 28:04](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1684)).

Jeremy Rose found that lowering the stakes cured perfectionism. He had torpedoed most of his earlier projects by deciding they would never be good enough; he built his Cataclysm guide in 15-minute gaps during his newborn daughter's naps, and caring for her made imperfect fonts and layouts obviously unimportant ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 22:10](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1330)).

**In practice:**

- Write down why you are making this game and why your last one stopped ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 4:06](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=246)).
- Add one new thing every working day; do not count tweaks ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:26](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=326)).
- Keep two or three tasks in different disciplines to rotate between ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 7:49](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=469); [Phillip Daigle 2020, 13:26](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=806)).
- Prefer a small, regular slice of time to occasional bursts ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 15:04](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=904)).
- Step away before deciding whether to throw work out, and keep old versions to compare against ([Joel Ryan 2022, 26:16](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1576); [Joel Ryan 2022, 28:04](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1684)).
- Keep a credits file from day one ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 16:42](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1002)).

## Long-lived roguelikes: maintainers, legacy code, rewrites and variants

Some roguelikes live for decades. ADOM has been developed by its creator since 1992 ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 2:06](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=126)), while Angband passed to non-creators almost at once ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 3:56](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=236)) and NetHack's DevTeam was built from contributors ([Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 3:56](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=236)). That creates production problems most games never face: what to do with an engine that has outgrown itself, who gets to change a game players have loved for twenty years, and how to keep volunteers coming.

### Content is the real asset

Biskup's central lesson from ADOM is that writing the content, not the engine, is the real work. When he built a modern Java successor, JADE, he found ADOM had so much content that could not be ported that moving it would take five years or more, so it was easier to bring JADE's good ideas back into ADOM ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 24:06](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1446)). The same reasoning drives his later plans: use ADOM as an engine for other games, reusing its body of content with very different gameplay, as in an unreleased mobile prototype called ADOM the Arena ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 24:45](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1485)). Ultimate ADOM extends it further, using its story as a reason to build variants for different platforms and play styles on one unified engine, so players learn the rules once and carry that knowledge between games ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 11:24](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=684)).

### Rewrite, restart or glue

Whether to rewrite is where the talks pull apart, and Biskup's own history is the case study. Disliking ADOM's architecture, he spent what little programming time he had on JADE, which further stalled ADOM ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 15:21](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=921)). Yet by 2017, after 25 years of code, many ideas for ADOM were technically almost impossible or not worth the effort, and players' suggestions kept hitting the engine's limits; the team chose to build a new game, Ultimate ADOM, which Biskup insists is not ADOM 2 but something different ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 8:55](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=535)). He also tells would-be modders that if you have your own vision, writing a new roguelike is often easier than modifying ADOM's sources, which his own team finds really hard ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 27:31](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1651)).

Ritchie argues the other side for projects still in development: do not throw a project away to start over just because you have learned enough to do it better; keep the existing code malleable and work with it ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:41](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=341)). Tarn Adams gives a third option from Dwarf Fortress, which he describes as having a geological history of layers piled on each other. Look for features you can build by gluing together systems you already have; the villains feature reuses existing monsters, necromancer apprentices, spying agents and relationships, and cutting corners this way saves years. He says the approach would work in a more pared-down game with comparable pieces too ([Tarn Adams 2018, 4:06](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=246)).

The positions fit together once you separate engine from content. Biskup's rewrite stalled the game when it meant moving content to a new engine ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 15:21](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=921); [Thomas Biskup 2016, 24:06](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1446)); the new start he did commit to was a different game, built for ideas the old engine could not hold ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 8:55](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=535)). Ritchie's warning is about restarting the same game because you could now write it better ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:41](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=341)). Adams' approach is what to do when you stay: treat the accumulated layers as building material ([Tarn Adams 2018, 4:06](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=246)).

### Who may change a game players love

Erik Osheim and Robert Au describe the maintainer's position on Angband. Angband was maintained by non-creators very early: its creators graduated in 1990, and the first public release in 1993 came from other students. Maintainers get less leeway for drastic changes than original creators, because veteran players are attached to old versions (on IRC people still argue that the last good version was 1997, or 2005) and ask whether the original author would approve ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 3:56](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=236)). Yet volunteers on an unpaid game need room to make their own mark; most will not volunteer just to fix bugs. Outside pressures force change anyway, such as Angband running on small Android screens ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 4:32](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=272)).

> Most people don't want to just volunteer to go fix bugs all the time; they want to do things, they want to make their own mark on the game. — [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 4:32](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=272)

Nick McConnell, a later Angband maintainer, offers the escape valve: fork the game into a new variant. That frees a developer from the original's baggage, and players who are hard on changes to the original tend to welcome variants warmly, even buggy ones ([Nick McConnell 2021, 8:54](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=534)). Maintenance also means subtracting. The Angband team removed little-used options and old ports it could not test, since features nobody uses produce no bug reports and cannot be maintained; that was somewhat controversial with the few people who still used them ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 15:44](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=944)).

### Governance

Long-lived roguelikes have settled on very different structures. Angband shows how a single-maintainer model breaks. When Robert Rühlmann burned out after about five years of unpaid work, a dead zone of roughly a year and a half followed; the announced successor released nothing, and Andi Sidwell, who had been releasing unofficial versions, became maintainer when Nick McConnell declared it and nobody objected ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 7:32](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=452)). Sidwell, from the open-source world, then moved Angband from a benevolent dictator to a collaborative team with a public issue tracker, public version control and a relicence to GPLv2 that meant contacting more than 100 contributors, though what vanilla Angband should be, museum piece or living game, stayed open ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 9:52](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=592)).

NetHack's DevTeam grew from contributors. Players posted bug-fix diffs on Usenet, then tested feature patches, and strong contributors were invited in; Jesse Collet joined in 1988 after posting suggestions with tested code ([Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 3:56](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=236)). The team had no real leader and no code ownership, ideas arrived as "here is what I coded", and Collet realised in hindsight that they never said "no" or "but", only "yes, and", improving on what had been done ([Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 6:40](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=400)). Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead took openness furthest: Jeremy Rose says it began as Zachary Jenkins' solo project and has had over 1,700 contributors, which he compares to Python's roughly 2,000, making it "nobody's game", an amalgam of many people's ideas ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 4:44](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=284)). bhauth sees the design result of that kind of history in Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup: built and tested by many people over a long time, its design philosophy is the overlap of several perspectives rather than one framework, such as removing or automating no-brainer choices where one option is strictly better but more annoying. His advice is not to be ideological, because a blend of heuristics usually beats one ([bhauth 2020, 17:58](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=1078)).

### When the developer goes quiet

ADOM's long gap shows the failure mode. Around 2001 Biskup co-founded an IT company and worked 60–80-hour weeks while the code had outgrown itself; exhausted, the first thing he stopped was communicating with players, and a PhD and marriage cut his time further. There were two releases in almost a decade, the last at the end of 2002 ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 15:14](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=914)). What brought it back was, in part, that the players were still there ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 17:22](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1042)).

**In practice, for maintainers and successors:**

- Treat the content as the asset; prefer moving ideas into the existing game over moving content to a new engine ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 24:06](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1446)).
- Before a rewrite, ask whether you are rebuilding the same game or making a new one the old engine cannot hold ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 8:55](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=535); [Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:41](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=341)).
- Build new features from systems you already have where you can ([Tarn Adams 2018, 4:06](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=246)).
- Expect less leeway than the creator had; put radical ideas into a variant ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 3:56](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=236); [Nick McConnell 2021, 8:54](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=534)).
- Give volunteers room to make their mark, and make the path from patch to team visible ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 4:32](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=272); [Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 3:56](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=236)).
- Plan succession before burnout, with public tracking and version control so others can carry on ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 7:32](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=452); [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 9:52](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=592)).
- Remove what you cannot test ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 15:44](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=944)).
- If you must slow down, keep talking to players ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 15:14](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=914)).

## Tensions and open questions

**Start small, or make what you want?** Zapata, Ge and Lait argue for a small finished game first, because finishing is how you learn and how you get feedback ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 4:14](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=254); [Josh Ge 2018, 4:16](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=256); [Jeff Lait 2025, 3:20](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=200)). Daigle deliberately ignored that advice on Rogue's Gate, arguing that a game made purely for yourself has no pressure to relieve and is better treated as creative expression ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 23:34](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1414)). The choice depends on whether the goal is a game other people play or the act of making it.

**How much to decide before you start.** Yano's two-page design document and Daigle's discard-heavy exploration leave most of the game to discovery ([Casey Yano 2022, 11:04](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=664); [Phillip Daigle 2020, 21:22](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1282)); White wants resource mechanics settled up front because everything gets designed around them, and Zapata set explicit guidelines at the start ([Dylan White 2021, 2:31](https://youtu.be/kvgKKRLil_8?t=151); [Santiago Zapata 2016, 5:24](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=324)). Daigle himself says his approach would be a horrible idea commercially ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 21:22](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1282)). The useful question is which of your systems are foundational enough that changing them later throws away work.

**How long code should live.** Yano kept Slay the Spire's code decoupled and deleted freely ([Casey Yano 2022, 12:00](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=720)); Cronin watched Monster Train's real-time prototype code carry into a turn-based game and cause problems, and later argued that even small multi-month roguelikes deserve planned architecture ([Brian Cronin 2021, 5:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=305); [Brian Cronin 2024, 4:57](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=297)). Yet Ritchie warns against throwing a project away to start over because you could now write it better ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:41](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=341)). Disposable code, planned code and kept code each have a defender, and none of these talks says how to recognise the moment a prototype becomes production.

**Rewrite, restart or glue.** Biskup's JADE rewrite stalled ADOM, yet he later started Ultimate ADOM as a new game because the old engine could not hold the ideas players wanted ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 15:21](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=921); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 8:55](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=535)); Tarn Adams prefers gluing together layers that already exist ([Tarn Adams 2018, 4:06](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=246)). Separating engine from content reconciles some of this, but whether a twenty-five-year codebase should be extended or replaced remains a judgment each long-lived project makes alone.

**A tight core or a city.** Ritchie, Billingsley and the Against the Storm team cut whatever does not serve the core or make runs differ ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 4:48](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=288); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 11:06](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=666); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 7:51](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=471)). Moromisato's "build a city instead of a resort" and Day's kitchen-sink Shadow of the Worm value accumulated, mismatched content ([George Moromisato 2016, 26:49](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1609); [Darren Grey et al. 2020, 19:03](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=1143)), though even NetHack's city cut a Jedi class, and Moromisato is unsure that was right ([George Moromisato 2016, 24:41](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1481)). The choice depends on time horizon: the city takes decades.

**Is fun the final test?** Ge's rule is that if the core minute-to-minute play is not fun, nothing else matters ([Josh Ge 2018, 5:50](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=350)). Nelson argues that following the fun uncritically means following implications rather than deciding on them, and that a less fun design you can stand behind is sometimes the right one ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 10:49](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=649)). The two can coexist, fun as a requirement and not a sufficient justification, but the talks do not say where the line falls.

**Silent observation or active listening.** Biskup and DiIorio watch without explaining or steering ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 19:09](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1149); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 11:52](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=712)); Cronin rejects total silence and talks as an active listener ([Brian Cronin 2025, 23:38](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1418)). Silence suits tests of onboarding and interface, where the question is what a stranger does alone; active listening suits tests of the player's reasoning.

**Who should test.** Subset uses other developers and people who know its work for its hardcore-first builds ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 8:14](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=494)); Cronin warns against over-relying on game developers ([Brian Cronin 2025, 18:47](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=1127)); Biskup keeps power players away from early-game tuning while needing them for the late game ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 32:47](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1967)). The right tester depends on what the build is testing.

**Developing in public, and its limits.** Players see what developers cannot, and a game shaped by them can be better for it ([Chris King 2022, 2:47](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=167); [Alice Lai 2021, 22:33](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1353)). But King points out that a long early access community stops representing first-time players, and calls finding newcomer feedback a tough, open question ([Chris King 2022, 15:10](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=910)).

**What data can tell you.** Liotta learned quickly from public play metrics on which levels players enjoyed and where they got stuck ([Colin Liotta 2018, 10:12](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=612)); the Against the Storm team warns that pick rates reward dull perks and bury interesting situational ones, and pairs data with targeted beta questions ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 14:18](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=858); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 12:17](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=737)). In these two cases, metrics served well for which levels players enjoyed and where they got stuck, and misled when pick rates were read as a measure of what is interesting.

**New systems or fixing old ones.** Blaseball puts new systems ahead of repairing broken ones, partly to stay unpredictable and partly because rebuilding costs more ([Joel Clark 2020, 14:24](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=864)). DiIorio warns that design problems left in place become harder to change as players grow attached ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 8:13](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=493)). Debenham's short update cycle softens the dilemma by making any single experiment cheap to revisit ([Evan Debenham 2021, 7:34](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=454)).

**Should every bug be fixed?** Monster Train's success is credited to consistent triage ([Brian Cronin 2021, 18:11](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1091)). Grinblat asks whether games built from colliding systems should make explicit room for bugs that enchant, while admitting that turning a bug into a feature is labour only some bugs can get ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 4:07](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=247); [Jason Grinblat 2021, 26:43](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1603)). How to decide which ones is left open here.

**Unsolved production problems.** Making procedural text templates easy to author and localise is still open for the Caves of Qud team ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:56:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6982)). Perry does not know how to keep the experimental freedom of a fifty-game collection inside a single game ([Jon Perry 2025, 39:00](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=2340)). And Angband's maintainers left open whether a decades-old vanilla game should be a museum piece or a living game ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 9:52](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=592)).

## Checklist

- Is this the game you can finish, or the dream project? If it is the dream, have you shipped something small first ([Josh Ge 2018, 4:16](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=256))?
- Can you state the core mechanic in one sentence, or name the feeling the game is for, and have you prototyped that alone ([Josh Ge 2018, 5:50](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=350); [Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 15:17](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=917))?
- Which of your systems (a spell resource, say) will everything else be designed around, and have you settled them early ([Dylan White 2021, 2:31](https://youtu.be/kvgKKRLil_8?t=151))?
- Are there values or implications in your numbers and categories that you would not stand behind, however fun they make the game ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 20:00](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1200))?
- What is the cheapest medium that answers your current question, and have you decided when this prototype's code stops being disposable ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 2:00](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=120); [Brian Cronin 2024, 4:57](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=297))?
- For every planned system: do you need it even though the genre expects it, is it worth the time, does it distract from the core, could another system do its job, and does it make runs differ ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 11:06](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=666); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 16:44](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1004); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 7:51](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=471))?
- Does each ambitious feature have an escape hatch, a simple version it can collapse to if it fails ([Tarn Adams 2018, 20:43](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1243))?
- Have you multiplied your estimate by four, twice, and kept the release year off the trailer ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 10:37](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=637); [Tyler Coleman 2024, 2:34](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=154))?
- If you are generating content, have you budgeted for quality, validation and localisation, and compared each generator's cost with its effect on the player ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 22:48](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1368); [Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 33:10](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1990))?
- When did someone who did not build the game last play it while you watched, and what changed as a result ([Brian Cronin 2025, 7:40](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=460); [Brian Cronin 2025, 15:26](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=926))?
- Can a player report a bug with one key, with logs and save attached, and does someone read every report ([Brian Cronin 2021, 16:25](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=985); [Brian Cronin 2021, 18:11](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1091))?
- When players ask for a fix, have you identified the problem behind it, and said publicly when the answer is no ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 17:23](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1043); [Chris King 2022, 10:09](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=609))?
- How long does it take to add one more item, spell or monster, and who is waiting on whom ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 8:11](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=491); [Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 3:51](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=231))?
- Did you add something new on your last working day, and do you know why your previous projects stopped ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:26](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=326); [Matt Ritchie 2017, 4:06](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=246))?
- If you stepped away tomorrow, could someone else carry the game on, and would your players hear from you ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 9:52](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=592); [Thomas Biskup 2016, 15:14](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=914))?
